name: Leontius Scholasticus
bio: Leontius Scholasticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 6 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 149, 150, 571, 573, 575, 579).

poems.title: Book VII, 149: On the Same
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: The Telamonian lies low in Troy, but he gave no foeman cause to boast of his death. For Time finding no other man worthy of such a deed entrusted it to his own self-slaying hand.

poems.title: Book VII, 150: On the Same
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: Ajax lieth in Troy after a thousand vaunted deeds of prowess, blaming not his foes but his friends.

poems.title: Book VII, 571
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: When Orpheus departed, perchance some Muse survived, but at thy death, Plato, the lyre ceased to sound. For in thy mind and in thy fingers there yet survived some little fragment at least of ancient music.

poems.title: Book VII, 573
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: This is the tomb of Cheiredius whom the Attic land nourished, an orator the image of the ancient ten, ever easily convincing the judge, but when himself a judge never swerving a hair's breadth from the straight path.

poems.title: Book VII, 575
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: The tomb is Rhode’s. She was a Tyrian woman, and quitting her country came to this city for the sake of her children. She adorned the bed of Gemellus of eternal memory, who formerly was a professor of law in this city. She died in old age, but should have lived for thousands of years: we never feel we have enough of the good.

poems.title: Book VII, 579
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: Thou seest the ever-smiling face of Peter the orator, excellent in debate, excellent in friendship. In the theatre whilst looking at the performance he fell from the roof with others and was the only one who died, after surviving a short time, sufficient for his needs. I call this no violent death, but a natural one.

poems.title: Book IX, 614: On a small Bath next that called Zeuxippus
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: Be not wrath, Zeuxippus, with this bath that arises next thee. The little star called Erotylus shines sweetly though next the Great Bear.

poems.title: Book IX, 624: On another Bath next the Public Baths in Byzantium
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: A citizen built me at the gate of the public bath for excellence, not for competition. Let that serve many; I supply water and scent and charm to an intimate few.

poems.title: Book IX, 630: On the Royal Hot Baths
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: These are really the royal hot baths, for our fathers, admiring them, gave them this name. By no mortal fire is the bright water warmed, but the spring is born hot of its own accord. Nor dost thou require a cold stream for the bath, but tempered as thou dost desire it, it gushes forth.

poems.title: Book IX, 650: On an Inn situated between the Zeuxippus and the Hippodrome
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: On the one side I have close by me the Zeuxippus, a pleasant bath, and on the other the race-course. After seeing the races at the latter and taking a bath in the former, come and rest at my hospitable table. Then in the afternoon you will be in plenty of time for the other races, reaching the course from your room quite near at hand.

poems.title: Book IX, 681: On a Shell with a Carving of Aphrodite
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: It is a great favour I grant thee, Dionysus. Cypris bathes in me, and from her I bring thee the cup.

poems.title: Book XVI, 33: On a Portrait of Callinicus the Cubicularius
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: Thou conquerest in beauty of soul as much as in beauty of face, for thou possessest everything that is worthy of thy name, and ever in the bed-chamber, sending the emperor to sleep, thou dost sow all gentleness in his ears.

poems.title: Book XVI, 37
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: Thou seest Peter in his golden robes, and the Provinces that stand by him witness to his successive labours; the first is a witness of the East, and the pair after her are witnesses of the purple shell, and again of the East.

poems.title: Book XVI, 245: On a Statue of a Satyr
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: Dionysus, seeing the Satyr in such pain, and pitying him, made him into stone, but not even so did he cease from his anguish ill to bear; but even though he be stone he still suffers, the luckless creature.

poems.title: Book XVI, 272: On a Picture of the Physician Iamblichus
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: This is Iamblichus, sweetest among men, who reached old age without knowing the converse of Aphrodite; but practising medicine and teaching his skill to others, he did not hold out his hand to receive even righteous gain.

poems.title: Book XVI, 357: On the Same
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.text: Cytherea loved Anchises, and Selene Endymion, so it is fabled by men of old time. But now a new fable shall be sung, that Victory, it seems, fell in love with the eyes and chariot of Porphyrius.

poems.title: The Death of Music (Mackail)
poems.author: Leontius Scholasticus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: When Orpheus was gone, a Muse was yet haply left, but when thou didst perish, Plato, the harp likewise ceased; for till then there yet lived some little fragment of the old melodies, saved in thy soul and hands.
